newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Labuan makes strides as offshore centre - official.
newsitem.headline: Labuan makes strides as offshore centre - official.

text.p: Labuan has made significant strides as an offshore banking centre, the head of the Malaysian island's financial service authority said on Thursday.

The government has issued 54 banking licences in Labuan over the last several years, Awang Adek Hussain, director-general of the Labuan Offshore Financial Service Authority and assistant director of Bank Negara, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
There also has been a tremendous increase in interest from insurance companies, he said.
"We are encouraged and think that this rapid trend in the increase in offshore companies will increase in the future," said Awang.
Labuan, an island off eastern Sabah state in Borneo, was established as an offshore financial centre in 1990.

It has become more attractive since a government decision last year to repeal the withholding tax exemption on most offshore borrowings. Only issues launched through Labuan entities are eligible for the exemption.

"The recent removal of the approved loan status is another measure to promote Labuan in the sense that now if there are funds raised through Labuan, withholding tax will not be applied, whereas if it is raised outside Labuan, the withholding tax will apply," Awang said.
Other measures also will boost Labuan as an offshore centre.
For example, foreign investment banks that wish to lead manage the debt issues of Malaysian companies now must have a presence in Labuan, Awang said.
"There is a requirement that you must be physically present in Labuan," he said.

And while there is some flexibility on the degree of involvement that a foreign investment bank must demonstrate in Labuan at the initial stage, "certainly physical presence in Labuan is a prerequisite," he said.
A few U.S. investment banks reportedly have formed joint ventures with Malaysian companies in Labuan so as to remain eligible for management roles in international debt issues.
Salomon Brothers, which was joint lead manager on the US$1.9 billion Yankee bond issue for Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas) last year, has made efforts to set up a joint venture, sources said.
CS First Boston, the other lead manager of the Petronas deal, already has a branch in Labuan.
Union Bank of Switzerland, which has a branch in Labuan, reportedly won the mandate for a US$400 million Yankee bond for Tenaga Nasional Bhd, although UBS declined comment.

Awang said recent changes in rules concerning Labuan have "been for the better" because they have encouraged more entities, such as Malaysian companies and foreign investment banks, to set up shop in the centre.
He noted that the government is formulating a new law known as the Offshore Securities Industries Act that should spur further growth in Labuan.
The law is expected to be passed by year-end, he said.
